title: 2,387 photographs, 237 participants: documenting Colombia’s biodiversity through Wiki Loves Earth 2026
content:
Over two months, people across Colombia photographed landscapes, species, and protected areas for Wiki Loves Earth 2026. Together, 237 participants contributed 2,387 images to Wikimedia Commons—placing Colombia tenth internationally and second among participating Latin American countries.

But the numbers tell only part of the story. Behind those 2,387 images was a community effort built around photography, learning, partnerships, and a shared interest in documenting Colombia’s biodiversity as free knowledge.

There are places we know because we travel through them, species we discover when we learn to observe them, and territories we begin to value when we find new ways to tell their stories.

In 2026, the Wikimedia community in Colombia turned its attention to the country’s biodiversity through Wiki Loves Earth, the international photography competition that invites people to document natural areas and natural heritage and share these images as free knowledge on Wikimedia Commons.

title: Documenting Lampung’s Living Heritage: Inside WikiNgigel
content:
Traditional dance and music are not simply performances. They are living forms of cultural knowledge, carried through movement, music, memory, teaching, and community practice. Yet much of this knowledge remains difficult to discover online, particularly when it comes to high-quality audiovisual documentation that can be freely accessed, studied, reused, and connected to other forms of knowledge.

In Lampung, Indonesia, WikiNgigel was created to help address this gap.

Implemented by Komunitas Wikimedia Bandar Lampung through a Wikimedia Foundation Rapid Fund project, WikiNgigel focuses on documenting Lampung’s traditional dance and musical traditions and bringing that documentation into the Wikimedia ecosystem. The project combines field documentation, collaboration with cultural practitioners, Wikimedia Commons, Wikipedia, Wikimedia Incubator, community training, and public dissemination.

The project began from a simple observation: documenting cultural heritage is not only about creating photographs or videos. It is also about making sure that the resulting documentation becomes useful knowledge.

title: Culture Is the Lifeline of Our Communities, or How to Organize Events in a Country Grappling with Social Conflicts
content:
The Long Night of Museums is an initiative that began in Germany in 1997. This initiative has been held in the city of La Paz since 2007, and as of 2026, seven cities across Bolivia have joined in (El Alto, Santa Cruz de la Sierra, Tarija, Sucre, Cochabamba, as well as activities in Potosí and Beni).

The Bolivian Wikimedia team has been participating in this event for the past two years thanks to strategic coordination with the Flavio Machicado Viscarra Foundation. Through this collaboration, we have fostered the spirit of the event by organizing games, challenges, snacks, and activities that highlight Wikipedia as an open educational resource and introduce visitors to figures from both contemporary and traditional Bolivian history.

Usually, this is a night when the whole city comes alive, with a wide range of cultural activities on offer. Movie theaters, museums, bookstores, cultural venues, restaurants, and independent artists take to the streets and organize events such as fairs, concerts, and performances. It goes without saying that this day has a significant economic and social impact—cities simply feel more alive.

title: SoKiD 2.0: Bringing the Kadazandusun Language into the Digital World through Wiktionary
content:
What if a word we add today becomes part of the digital heritage of the Kadazandusun language for generations to come?

On 9th September 2026, 70 students from 15 primary schools across Sabah gathered at Sekolah Kebangsaan Tengkurus in Kota Belud with a purpose that may seem simple, but carries great significance: to document Kadazandusun vocabulary in the digital world through Wiktionary.

This was SoKiD 2.0, short for Sompuruan Komi Boros Kadazandusun, or Kadazandusun Vocabulary Group.

Kadazandusun is one of the major languages spoken by communities in Sabah. However, like many heritage languages, its use among younger generations faces various challenges.

In schools, students may still have a limited command of basic vocabulary. Some may recognise a word but have difficulty understanding its meaning, context, or how to use it in a sentence. When vocabulary is limited, learning, writing, and communicating in one’s mother tongue can also become more challenging.

This is where SoKiD takes a different approach.

Rather than simply memorising words, students are encouraged to identify, understand, edit, and document Kadazandusun vocabulary themselves in the digital world through Wiktionary.
snippet: What if a word we add today becomes part of the digital heritage of the Kadazandusun language for generations to come?
creator: Jurina Jonimin

title: Inside the Heritage Month campaign to fill Wikipedia’s language void, one article at a time
content:
The instruction was simple, and Matete Lesele had given it many times. Choose an article on the English Wikipedia, he told the students in front of him, and translate it into the language you grew up speaking. Most reached for the wiki in their mother tongue. This student reached for Afrikaans; not her mother tongue. When he pointed her back toward her own language, she told him she couldn’t write it — the school she had gone to never taught her how.

Lesele, a librarian at the City of Johannesburg and a board member of Wikimedia South Africa, repeats some version of that exchange to almost everyone who asks why he does this work. It was the moment a vague worry turned specific. A language can live in conversation, in songs, in the things a grandmother says that no one writes down. But a person who cannot write their own language is unlikely to add it to the places people now go to look — and the largest of those, by a distance hard to overstate, is the one he spends his evenings inside.

title: Visa & Health: Your Passport to Wiki Indaba 2026 in Abidjan
content:
Members of the Wikimedia community and the African diaspora, preparations for Wiki Indaba 2026 in Abidjan are well underway!

To make sure your journey goes as smoothly as possible, it is important to start taking care of your travel and administrative requirements now.

Here are the two key steps you need to take to enter Côte d’Ivoire:

If you are a citizen of a ECOWAS member country (such as Nigeria, Ghana, Senegal, Mali, and others), you do not need a visa to enter Côte d’Ivoire. A valid passport or national identity card is sufficient.

For citizens of other African countries and members of the African diaspora living outside the ECOWAS region, a visa is required to enter Côte d’Ivoire.

The Ivorian government offers a straightforward electronic visa process:

  • Submit your application exclusively through the official website: snedai.com
  • Complete the application form and pay the visa fee online.
  • Print the “Pre-registration Letter” you receive by email. This document is required to board your flight. Your physical visa will be issued upon arrival at Abidjan airport.

    • Côte d’Ivoire has strict requirements regarding yellow fever vaccination.

title: Central and Eastern Europe’s Premier Free Knowledge Conference Debuts in Romania: Wikimedia CEE Meeting 2026 to Convene in Cluj-Napoca
content:
CLUJ-NAPOCA, Romania — For the first time in its history, Romania will host the annual regional conference of the Wikipedia movement: Wikimedia CEE Meeting 2026. Taking place from September 18 to 20, 2026, at Babeș-Bolyai University in Cluj-Napoca, the meeting brings together digital rights advocates, researchers, open-knowledge contributors, and chapter delegates from across Central and Eastern Europe and surrounding regions.

The event is organised by Wikimedians of Romania and Moldova User Group in partnership with Făgăraș Research Institute and hosted by Babeș-Bolyai University through its Faculty of European Studies, Office for Open Science, Centre for Students with Disabilities, and the Doctoral School “History. Culture. Civilisation.”

title: Growing from Wiki Club to Becoming a Community Towards the Future
content:
Reflections on the Wikimedia Malaysia 2026 Strategic Direction Conference

After discovering the Wikimedia platform, I began my journey of promoting and preserving my community’s language, Kadazandusun, through my participation in Wiki Club Kent. The club gave me an opportunity to learn more about the Wikimedia movement and to contribute to the world of free knowledge.

Today, that journey continues with the same mission. Although my time as a student and as a Wiki Club member has come to an end, my passion for contributing remains. I hope to take the Kadazandusun language further into the world as part of this community.

On 30th August 2026, I had the opportunity to participate in the Malaysian Wikimedia Strategy Summit 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, which brought together Wikimedians and community leaders from diverse backgrounds across Malaysia. For me, this was more than just a conference. It was a space for us to pause, reflect on the journey we have taken so far, and envision where the Malaysian Wikimedia community wants to go next.
snippet: Reflections on the Wikimedia Malaysia 2026 Strategic Direction Conference
creator: Jurina Jonimin

title: Women, the Sundanese Language, and Wikimedia Projects
content:
In our daily life, there are things we do not notice while they are still around us. A mother tongue can be one of them. We grow up hearing it at home, in conversations with family,  jokes exchanged between neighbours, or stories told before bedtime. We rarely stop to think about how many of our memories are carried by the words we inherit. However, when those words begin to disappear, we do realize that a language is never simply a collection of vocabulary, It is a way of remembering who we are.

I am a Sundanese woman, and Sundanese is part of the memory. 

For me, the question of whether the Sundanese language will continue to live is not merely a linguistic question. It is a deeply personal one. It is connected to the kind of world we will leave behind for the generations that come after us. Will they still be able to read old expressions, understand the stories told by their grandparents, recognize the names of plants and places in their own language? Or they simply have the freedom to say, “This is my language.”

content:

Weekly highlight

  • The Future Audiences team has started a discussion on English Wikipedia about a proposed new experiment to show a temporary notice about the new Google Preferred Sources feature to Wikipedia readers coming from Google. The experiment is to test whether this notice makes visitors come back to Wikipedia more often. Preferred Sources feature lets users choose websites they trust so Google can highlight content from those sources more prominently in Search and AI experiences. We are interested in testing this on other languages that Google supports and would welcome assistance with starting conversations on other wikis. If interested, please reach out to Future Audiences on the talk page.

title: CEE Beyond the Crossroads: Wikimedia CEE Meeting 2026 Convenes in Cluj-Napoca
content:
From September 18 to 20, 2026, Wikimedians, open-knowledge researchers, and free-culture advocates from Central and Eastern Europe—and increasingly Central Asia—gather for the first time in Cluj-Napoca, Romania, for the Wikimedia CEE Meeting 2026. 

Hosted by Wikimedians of Romania and Moldova User Group in partnership with Făgăraș Research Institute and Babeș-Bolyai University (UBB), this year’s regional conference marks a defining step forward for one of the most interconnected community networks in the Wikimedia movement. 

Under the slogan “CEE Beyond the Crossroads,” the meeting signals a profound shift: moving past reactive survival amid geopolitical and digital fragmentation toward long-term regional resilience, institutional empowerment, and intentional cooperation.

title: African Wikipedian Alliance (AWA) Fellowship Reflections: Learning Through Pan-Africanism by Daniel Damilola Obiokeke
content: I began the African Wikipedian Alliance European Partnership for Democracy Digital Democracy Initiative (EPD-DDI) Enhancing Youth Voices and Youth Civic Engagement in a Secured Digital Space through it Digitise Youth fellowship thinking I already understood the terrain. I had worked in Wikimedia spaces before, led communities, and supported projects that reached beyond Nigeria, so I assumed this experience would mainly extend across my technical process for finding topics, identifying red links, and guiding contributors toward strong articles. What I did not expect was that the deepest lesson of the fellowship would not be about editing tools at all. It would be about how knowledge moves across Africa, and how often that movement is interrupted by language, sourcing barriers, and the unequal conditions under which some references are required to be documented.
